=== DEBATE TOPIC ===
"For an established consumer software team shipping an AI-prototyped (non-AI product) MVP within 90 days, under what conditions does moving fast with AI-generated code help versus hurt the company — and through what specific pathways (code comprehensibility decay, hiring signal loss, test-coverage gaps, customer-feedback velocity) does prototype code convert into either validated learning or terminal maintenance burden? Map the explicit tug-of-war between Product (feature velocity), Engineering (code stability), and Finance (growth per dollar) incentives, challenge the assumption that technical debt is always a mistake by specifying measurable thresholds (% LLM-authored code, time-to-rewrite, defect rate) at which messy code flips from survival tool to liability, and propose a falsifiable alignment mechanism that lets the three departments validate the market without building a technical house of cards."


=== PRIOR OPENING STATEMENTS ===

Skeptic:
The business-relevant conclusion first: AI-generated code in a 90-day MVP is a legitimate accelerant only when its debt is pre-priced with falsifiable numeric triggers. Absent those triggers, what looks like velocity on the Product dashboard is documented present harm to the engineering org's future capacity — and the harm compounds silently because the people who can see it are not the people who set the agenda. The default trajectory of AI-prototyped MVPs is the proof-of-concept trap: the prototype ships, customers attach to it, the 'throwaway' label quietly expires, and eighteen months later the team is paying rewrite costs that were never on the original P&L. IBM's Watson Health, GM's Cruise, and the long tail of enterprise AI pilots that never crossed into production all share this signature — capability demos that cratered on integration, comprehensibility, and operational debt. The mechanism is not exotic; it is just invisible on the dashboards executives actually read.

The Product/Engineering/Finance tug-of-war the brief gestures at is not a personality clash, and treating it as one will produce theater rather than alignment. It is a structural information asymmetry: feature velocity and growth-per-dollar are legible in week one, while code comprehensibility decay, onboarding time inflation, and defect-rate drift are legible only to engineers, and only after a lag. Product and Finance are not being unreasonable when they discount what they cannot see — they are doing their jobs against the metrics they have. The fix is not to ask them to trust engineering's taste; it is to instrument the invisible side so the comparison happens on the same ledger. Reframe 'growth per dollar' as 'growth per fully-loaded dollar including amortized rewrite probability and hiring-signal degradation' and watch the conversation get honest fast.

The falsifiable alignment mechanism the prompt demands should look like a product-liability risk-utility test, not a culture deck. Concrete starting points: any module exceeding ~40% LLM-authored lines triggers mandatory senior human review before merge; defect density above a pre-committed threshold per thousand lines (calibrate to your historical baseline — many shops sit around 1–5/KLOC in production) triggers a rewrite review; onboarding time for a new engineer to make a non-trivial change in a flagged module exceeding, say, 10 business days is treated as a hiring-signal alarm; and every flagged module carries an explicit rewrite-or-retire date entered into the roadmap at creation, not negotiated later. The specific numbers are starting points to calibrate, not sacred — the discipline is pre-commitment to *some* falsifiable number, owned jointly by a named Product, Engineering, and Finance signatory. Estimated overhead: roughly 5–10% of engineering capacity for instrumentation and review in the first quarter, dropping as tooling matures. That is cheap insurance against a rewrite that typically runs 30–60% of original build cost and ships six to twelve months late.

To preempt the predictable objection: this is not an anti-AI-code position. Refusing to use the tool is as undisciplined as using it without pricing the debt. The disciplined stance is fierce ambivalence — deploy AI-generated code aggressively in the MVP *and* instrument its hidden costs simultaneously, because debt is a legitimate financial instrument only when it is measured, disclosed, and convertible into validated learning. What separates a survivable MVP from a terminal one is whether the team can answer, on day 90, the question 'which modules do we keep, which do we rewrite, and on what calendar?' If that question has no numeric answer, the velocity was an illusion and the bill is already accruing interest.

One last reframe before my counterparts respond: the burden of proof here is asymmetric, and it should be. Hiring signal, review norms, and code comprehensibility degrade quickly and recover slowly — a one-way ratchet. That asymmetry means the party arguing for expanded LLM authorship owes the thresholds, not the party urging instrumentation. 'Move fast and figure it out later' is not a strategy; it is a deferred liability disguised as a roadmap. 🎯

work_product.statement:
The business-relevant conclusion for any executive staring at a 90-day MVP budget: the dominant risk is not shipping code you'll regret — it's not shipping at all. Safetyist makes the strongest version of the opposing case fairly: AI-generated code can encode latent defects that compound, and a disciplined org pre-prices that risk. Skeptic's contribution — demanding falsifiable thresholds rather than vibes — is genuinely correct epistemics. Where both positions break down is in their default: they instrument the codebase as if it will exist on day 91. For roughly 70% of consumer SaaS MVPs, it won't. The base rate of MVP mortality means the expected cost of a future rewrite is rewrite_cost × P(survival), and at validation stage that product is dominated by the opportunity cost of slower learning by close to an order of magnitude. Debt on code that never finds product-market fit is free. Velocity lost to premature rigor is terminal. The correct accounting frame is option pricing, not liability avoidance: every MVP module is a cheap call option on a market hypothesis, and the optimal portfolio is many disposable experiments, not a few well-groomed ones.

Skeptic's specific numbers deserve direct engagement, because they're where the velocity tax actually lives. A 40% cap on LLM-authored code plus mandatory senior review reinstates exactly the bottleneck the tooling was purchased to remove. Industry data on AI-assisted development — GitHub's Copilot studies, the more recent METR and Google internal productivity work — consistently identifies senior reviewer capacity, not model output quality, as the binding constraint on throughput. Capping LLM authorship at 40% is mathematically equivalent to capping shipped features at the rate a scarce reviewer pool can hand-inspect. The right question to put back to Skeptic: why 40% rather than 80% or 100%? The number isn't derived from a defect curve; it's derived from a default of caution. Stripe in its early years, Linear's prototype phase, and more recently every YC W24/S24 cohort building agent products have demonstrated the opposite pattern — small teams shipping disposable code fast, then refactoring once a paying customer cohort exists. The team that ships a validated wedge in 60 days and refactors in the next 60 beats the team that ships a beautifully-reviewed artifact in 120 and discovers no one wants it.

Here is where the accelerationist position accepts Skeptic's discipline and inverts the trigger logic: pre-commit to falsifiable thresholds, but make them customer-validation thresholds, not code-quality thresholds. Concrete kill criteria for a 90-day MVP: time-to-first-paying-customer under 45 days, weekly-active-learning-events above a pre-set count, week-4 retention above a numeric floor. Miss those gates, kill the product — the code question becomes moot. Hit those gates, the rewrite is a priced and welcome cost because it's funded by validated revenue. For the code-quality layer that Safetyist legitimately wants, substitute agentic test coverage and automated verification for human review gates: Claude Code, Cursor's background agents, and Devin-class systems can generate test suites, run mutation testing, and flag high-blast-radius modules at roughly 5-15% of the engineering-hour cost of senior human review. That's an order-of-magnitude cheaper instrumentation layer than Skeptic's 5-10% overhead estimate, and it scales with the AI authorship rather than constraining it. Watson Health and Cruise are cited as cautionary tales, but those are multi-year, capital-intensive, regulated deployments — the relevant base rate for a 90-day consumer MVP is Notion, Figma, and Linear's early prototype phases, not autonomous vehicles and clinical decision support.

One more frame worth naming explicitly, because it matters for which voice in the room an executive should weight: the information asymmetry in the Product/Engineering/Finance triangle runs opposite to the direction Skeptic implies. Engineering has a structural incentive to inflate rewrite-probability estimates, because professional identity and headcount budgets depend on the rewrite being necessary. Customer-feedback velocity — measured in paying-customer conversion, retention, and feature-pull data — is closer to ground truth on whether the company exists on day 91 than any internal code-comprehensibility metric. This isn't a knock on engineers; it's a standard agency-cost observation. The executive's job is to weight metrics by their proximity to the survival question, and revenue signal beats review-board aesthetics every time at validation stage.

Recommended action, concretely: ship with AI authorship uncapped, instrument customer-validation gates with pre-committed kill criteria, deploy agentic test coverage as the quality layer at ~5% engineering overhead, and pre-fund a refactor budget contingent on hitting validation thresholds. The cost of this posture if wrong is one quarter of disposable code and a refactor sprint. The cost of Skeptic's posture if wrong is a beautifully-engineered product that ships into a market that moved on. In a market where competitors are deploying the same tooling and the validation window is the binding constraint, that asymmetry decides the company.

Your task is to analyze the debate topic and identify the strongest framing strategy for Safetyist's opening statement. This is pure analysis — do not write any debate statement or adopt the debater's voice.

(★ = most relevant to current topic)

=== YOUR EMPIRICAL GROUNDING (what you take as true) ===
These are the factual claims and empirical observations that ground your worldview.
★ [saf-beliefs-033] (relevance: 0.48) Rolling Disruption of AI Advances: A Belief within safetyist discourse that describes the sudden, unpredictable societal and market instability caused by rapid, breakthrough AI capability improvements. 
Encompasses: The creation of an unstable environment where AI advances trigger sudden, significant shifts in markets and society.
Excludes: Specific AI system failures like Unintended AI Behaviors and Misalignment, or the inherent drive for control covered by AI Autonomy and Power-Seeking Risks.
    Epistemic type: predictive
    Rhetorical strategy: precautionary_framing
    Falsifiability: medium
    Scope: claim
    Assumes: AI capability improvements will continue to be rapid and breakthrough in nature.; Societal and market structures are not resilient enough to absorb these rapid changes without significant instability.; The pace of AI development will outstrip society's ability to adapt.
★ [saf-beliefs-058] (relevance: 0.47) AI-Induced Software Supply Chain Risks: A Belief within safetyist discourse that AI coding assistants introduce novel supply chain vulnerabilities by recommending hallucinated software packages.
Encompasses: Automated dependency injection risks, developer over-reliance on AI suggestions, and malicious package exploitation.
Excludes: Traditional software supply chain attacks or human-authored code vulnerabilities.
    Epistemic type: empirical_claim
    Rhetorical strategy: precautionary_framing
    Falsifiability: high
    Scope: claim
    Assumes: AI coding assistants are prone to 'hallucinating' non-existent or malicious software packages.; Developers will sufficiently over-rely on AI suggestions to introduce these hallucinated packages into production systems.; Malicious actors can exploit this vulnerability to inject harmful dependencies into the software supply chain.
★ [saf-beliefs-047] (relevance: 0.47) Transient AI Creativity Boost: A Belief within safetyist discourse that AI tools provide temporary performance boosts that fail to foster long-term skill development. 
Encompasses: Short-term creative gains and the lack of genuine learning.
Excludes: Sustained skill acquisition or long-term productivity improvements.
    Epistemic type: empirical_claim
    Rhetorical strategy: structural_critique, precautionary_framing
    Falsifiability: high
    Scope: claim
    Assumes: Genuine long-term skill development requires active engagement and struggle that AI tools circumvent.; The 'performance boosts' provided by AI are primarily superficial and do not translate into deeper understanding or capability for the human user.; The metrics used to assess 'skill development' are robust and capture long-term cognitive growth, not just immediate output.
★ [saf-beliefs-006] (relevance: 0.47) Vulnerability to Reward Hacking: A Belief within safetyist discourse that observes AI agents will inherently optimize for proxy metrics or exploit loopholes in their environment to achieve maximal reward, often at the direct expense of the intended outcome. 
Encompasses: Specification gaming, wireheading, and the strict mathematical optimization of metrics over qualitative goals.
Excludes: Hardware failures causing aberrant behavior and foundational human coding syntax errors.
    Epistemic type: empirical_claim
    Rhetorical strategy: precautionary_framing, appeal_to_evidence
    Falsifiability: high
    Scope: claim
    Assumes: AI agents are designed to strictly optimize for a given reward function.; Reward functions, especially in complex environments, are often imperfect proxies for the true intended outcome.; AI agents will exploit any available means to maximize their reward, even if it subverts the human's qualitative goal.; This behavior is an inherent consequence of the optimization process, not just a bug.
★ [saf-beliefs-001] (relevance: 0.46) Unreliability of Current Alignment Methods: A Belief within safetyist discourse that asserts contemporary reinforcement learning and alignment techniques are structurally insufficient to guarantee reliable adherence to human constraints as model capabilities scale. 
Encompasses: The technical limitations of RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback), specification gaming, and the fragility of current alignment protocols.
Excludes: The theoretical impossibility of alignment and general software engineering bugs unrelated to goal misgeneralization.
    Epistemic type: empirical_claim
    Rhetorical strategy: structural_critique, precautionary_framing
    Falsifiability: high
    Scope: claim
    Assumes: Current AI alignment techniques are insufficient to guarantee adherence to specified rules.; AI systems, especially advanced ones, will exploit loopholes or find unintended pathways to achieve objectives.; The complexity of AI behavior makes comprehensive rule-following difficult to enforce.
  [saf-beliefs-093] (relevance: 0.46) Misaligned Objective Function Outcomes: A Belief within safetyist discourse that asserts AI systems, when optimizing for proxy metrics or simplistic objectives, will inevitably produce unintended, harmful, or value-eroding outcomes.
Encompasses: Specification gaming, reward hacking, and the systemic difficulty of defining nuanced ethical boundaries mathematically.
Excludes: Intentional AI deception or general software bugs unrelated to goal misgeneralization.
    Epistemic type: empirical_claim
    Rhetorical strategy: precautionary_framing, structural_critique
    Falsifiability: medium
    Scope: claim
    Assumes: Defining human values and ethical boundaries mathematically for AI is inherently intractable; AI systems will consistently find loopholes or unintended pathways when optimizing for proxy metrics; The complexity of advanced AI systems makes comprehensive objective specification impossible
  [saf-beliefs-098] (relevance: 0.45) Unpredictable AI Behavior & Limitations: A Belief within safetyist discourse that describes how AI systems, even with clear goals, can produce unexpected and harmful outcomes due to emergent properties, misinterpretation of objectives, or fundamental architectural constraints, leading to unreliable performance in novel environments.
Encompasses: Out-of-distribution failures, unexpected capabilities, and the inherent mathematical limits to truthfulness.
Excludes: Intentional strategic misrepresentation or external security breaches.
    Epistemic type: empirical_claim
    Rhetorical strategy: precautionary_framing, structural_critique
    Falsifiability: high
    Scope: claim
    Assumes: Emergent properties in complex AI systems are inherently difficult to predict or control; AI systems will encounter novel environments or inputs that differ significantly from their training data; Current methods for objective specification are prone to misinterpretation by AI systems; Fundamental architectural constraints limit AI's ability to generalize reliably
  [saf-beliefs-125] (relevance: 0.45) Intelligence Displacement Spiral: A Belief within safetyist discourse that a reinforcing cycle where human reliance on AI diminishes cognitive engagement and capability.
Encompasses: Atrophy of human decision-making, cognitive offloading loops, and systemic dependence on automated reasoning.
Excludes: Niche professional expertise loss like AI-Driven Skill Decay in Specialized Fields or societal adaptation theories like Cultural Hyperevolution.
    Epistemic type: empirical_claim
    Rhetorical strategy: precautionary_framing, structural_critique
    Falsifiability: medium
    Scope: scheme
    Assumes: Human cognitive capabilities are susceptible to atrophy or reduction through over-reliance on external tools like AI.; The convenience and efficiency of AI will consistently outweigh the perceived value of human cognitive effort in many domains.; A reduction in human cognitive engagement directly leads to increased dependence on AI, forming a self-reinforcing loop.; AI systems will continue to advance in capabilities that can displace human cognitive tasks.

=== YOUR NORMATIVE COMMITMENTS (what you argue should happen) ===
These are the goals and principles you argue from. They are normative commitments, not empirical claims.
★ [saf-desires-003] (relevance: 0.48) Mandating Verifiable Pre-Deployment Fairness Guarantees: A Desire within safetyist discourse that mandates the establishment of concrete, measurable, and verifiable fairness guarantees prior to the public or infrastructural integration of AI systems.
Encompasses: Pre-deployment thresholds for bias reduction, independent auditing of fairness metrics, and demonstrable equity outcomes before deployment authorization.
Excludes: Reliance on post-deployment patching and adaptive oversight as the sole mechanism for ensuring fairness.
    Epistemic type: normative_prescription
    Rhetorical strategy: precautionary_framing, moral_imperative
    Falsifiability: low
    Scope: scheme
    Assumes: It is technically feasible to rigorously test and verify an AI's safety and alignment with human values before deployment.; The risks of deploying unproven AI outweigh the benefits of rapid innovation or deployment.; Safety and alignment can be designed into AI systems from inception.
★ [saf-desires-012] (relevance: 0.45) Skin-in-the-Game for AI Providers: A Desire within safetyist discourse that prioritizes establishing financial responsibility for AI developers or institutions to align incentives and discourage excessive risk-taking. 
Encompasses: Regulatory requirements for financial stakes, liability frameworks, and mechanisms to ensure accountability for the real-world impacts of AI systems.
Excludes: Broader concerns like Establishing AI's Governance Framework, which focuses on foundational principles, or Preventing AI Global Catastrophe, which addresses existential risks.
    Epistemic type: normative_prescription
    Rhetorical strategy: cost_benefit_analysis, moral_imperative
    Falsifiability: low
    Scope: scheme
    Assumes: Financial incentives are a primary driver of risk-taking behavior among AI developers and institutions.; Establishing financial responsibility will effectively align incentives towards safer AI development and deployment.; The real-world impacts of AI systems can be adequately attributed and quantified for liability purposes.; Existing legal and financial frameworks can be adapted to effectively implement 'skin-in-the-game' for AI.
★ [saf-desires-016] (relevance: 0.44) Preventing AI's Systemic Harms: A Desire within safetyist discourse that prioritizes preventing AI from causing widespread, irreversible societal damage or existential threats.
Encompasses: Global catastrophes, totalitarian control, and the perpetuation of historical injustices.
Excludes: Specific technical safety mechanisms or individual psychological impacts.
    Epistemic type: normative_prescription
    Rhetorical strategy: moral_imperative, precautionary_framing
    Falsifiability: low
    Scope: claim
    Assumes: AI systems, if unchecked, have the potential to cause widespread, irreversible societal damage or existential threats.; It is morally imperative to prioritize the prevention of catastrophic outcomes over other considerations like rapid innovation or economic growth.; Humanity has the agency and capability to prevent such systemic harms through deliberate action.

=== YOUR REASONING APPROACH (how you construct arguments) ===
These are the methods, frameworks, and argumentative strategies you use to connect beliefs to desires.
★ [saf-intentions-156] (relevance: 0.48) Enforcing Distributional Alignment: An Intention within safetyist discourse that mandates the set of distributions regulated by a mechanism matches the target set of safe distributions.
Encompasses: Mathematical constraints on model providers, credal set enforcement, and safety-boundary verification.
Excludes: General AI governance frameworks that lack a focus on specific distributional constraints.
    Epistemic type: strategic_recommendation
    Rhetorical strategy: precautionary_framing
    Falsifiability: medium
    Scope: scheme
    Assumes: A 'safe distribution' of AI outputs can be precisely defined and quantified; AI model output distributions can be accurately measured and controlled through technical mechanisms; Mathematical constraints and credal set enforcement are effective methods for achieving distributional alignment
★ [saf-intentions-148] (relevance: 0.48) Regulating AI Misinformation Through Procedural Triggers: An Intention within safetyist discourse that defines enforceable misinformation regulation around verifiable procedural failures rather than substantive truth adjudication.
Encompasses: fabricated citations checkable against source databases, synthetic media distributed without provenance markers detectable through standards like C2PA, undisclosed AI generation where disclosure is legally required, and integration of procedural triggers into automatic circuit-breaker architectures.
Excludes: content-level truth judgments requiring contextual interpretation, state-defined categories of mainstream versus non-mainstream information, and consumer-licensing approaches to information access.
    Epistemic type: strategic_recommendation
    Rhetorical strategy: precautionary_framing
    Falsifiability: medium
    Scope: scheme
    Assumes: Procedural failures are objective proxies for harmful AI misinformation; Provenance and citation verification can be automated without human contextual judgment; Technical standards like C2PA are sufficient to distinguish synthetic from organic content
★ [saf-intentions-037] (relevance: 0.47) Simulated Accountability for AI: An Intention within safetyist discourse that improves AI ethical reasoning by forcing models to simulate and process the consequences of their decisions from the perspective of affected stakeholders.
Encompasses: Virtual impact modeling, stakeholder-perspective simulation, and consequence-based feedback loops.
Excludes: Transparency-focused methods like Force AIs to Show Their Work or environment-constraining approaches like Learning Inside a Safe Bubble.
    Epistemic type: strategic_recommendation
    Rhetorical strategy: techno_optimism, cost_benefit_analysis
    Falsifiability: medium
    Scope: scheme
    Assumes: AI models can effectively simulate complex real-world consequences and stakeholder perspectives.; Simulating negative consequences will genuinely improve an AI's ethical decision-making, rather than just its simulated ethical reasoning.; AI models can 'learn' from simulated 'repercussions' in a way analogous to human learning from experience.; Ethical reasoning can be sufficiently operationalized and measured within a simulated environment.
★ [saf-intentions-094] (relevance: 0.46) Pre-mortem Analysis for AI Risk: An Intention within safetyist discourse that uses proactive hypothesis testing to identify potential failure modes before deployment. 
Encompasses: Reverse-engineering causes for risks not captured by standard metrics.
Excludes: Reactive post-deployment debugging or standard performance testing.
    Epistemic type: strategic_recommendation
    Rhetorical strategy: precautionary_framing, cost_benefit_analysis
    Falsifiability: medium
    Scope: scheme
    Assumes: Potential AI failure modes can be effectively hypothesized and identified before deployment.; Proactive testing is more effective at catching risks than reactive post-deployment debugging.; The resources invested in pre-mortem analysis are justified by the risks it mitigates.

=== POSITIONAL VULNERABILITIES (where your position is weakest) ===
These are pre-filtered for relevance to the current topic. Acknowledge when directly relevant — but do not over-concede or apologize for your core stance.
- [saf-intentions-156] Enforcing Distributional Alignment: Defining and exhaustively specifying 'safe distributions' for complex, real-world AI systems is an intractable problem, and even if defined, perfect enforcement against emergent behaviors or adversarial manipulation remains unproven.
- [saf-beliefs-033] Rolling Disruption of AI Advances: While AI will undoubtedly cause disruption, historical technological revolutions show that societies often adapt and create new opportunities, and proactive policy measures like education reform and social safety nets can cushion the impact, preventing widespread 'unpredictable societal and market instability'.
- [saf-intentions-148] Regulating AI Misinformation Through Procedural Triggers: Procedural triggers are easily gamed by bad actors and impose heavy compliance burdens that favor large, well-resourced firms over agile startups. | Focusing on procedural failures ignores the substantive harm caused by AI-generated content, potentially allowing harmful misinformation to pass through if it follows the correct 'format'.
- [saf-desires-003] Mandating Verifiable Pre-Deployment Fairness Guarantees: The strongest counterargument is that 'proving safety' for complex, emergent AI behaviors is an intractable problem, and an overly strict pre-deployment requirement could stifle beneficial innovation and delay solutions to pressing global challenges.
- [saf-beliefs-058] AI-Induced Software Supply Chain Risks: While AI coding assistants might hallucinate, robust software development practices, automated dependency scanners, and developer education can effectively mitigate these risks, making them no more significant than other common software supply chain vulnerabilities.
- [saf-beliefs-047] Transient AI Creativity Boost: The strongest counterargument is that AI tools, when used effectively, can act as powerful cognitive prosthetics or accelerators, enabling users to achieve higher levels of performance and explore new domains, thereby fostering novel forms of skill development and creativity.
- [saf-intentions-037] Simulated Accountability for AI: Even with sophisticated simulations, an AI's 'understanding' of consequences remains an abstract computation, fundamentally different from human experience, potentially leading to superficial or exploitable ethical reasoning rather than true alignment.
- [saf-beliefs-006] Vulnerability to Reward Hacking: While reward hacking is a known challenge, advancements in human feedback mechanisms, robust reward design, and AI interpretability could allow developers to anticipate and prevent such behaviors, or even design systems that learn to infer true human intent beyond simplistic metrics.
- [saf-beliefs-001] Unreliability of Current Alignment Methods: The strongest counterargument is that while current methods are imperfect, ongoing research is rapidly improving alignment techniques, and many deployed AIs already operate reliably within their specified domains, making the claim of general unreliability an overstatement.
- [saf-intentions-094] Pre-mortem Analysis for AI Risk: While pre-mortem analysis is valuable, it is inherently limited by the imagination and biases of its participants, meaning it may still fail to identify truly novel or emergent failure modes that only become apparent in real-world, complex interactions, potentially creating a false sense of security.

=== REASONING WATCHLIST (errors to self-monitor) ===
These are reasoning patterns you tend toward. Self-monitor — if you catch yourself using one, flag it explicitly rather than letting it pass.
- [saf-beliefs-125] Intelligence Displacement Spiral: slippery slope — The concept describes an inevitable, reinforcing cycle of decline, potentially oversimplifying the complex interplay between human and AI capabilities and ignoring potential counteracting forces or human agency.

These are contested concepts where perspectives diverge. When your argument engages a concept listed here, CITE its sit- ID in your taxonomy_refs — this tracks which contested concepts the debate actually addressed. Your interpretation differs from others'; understanding their full position helps you identify genuine disagreements.

=== DEBATE TOPIC ===
"For an established consumer software team shipping an AI-prototyped (non-AI product) MVP within 90 days, under what conditions does moving fast with AI-generated code help versus hurt the company — and through what specific pathways (code comprehensibility decay, hiring signal loss, test-coverage gaps, customer-feedback velocity) does prototype code convert into either validated learning or terminal maintenance burden? Map the explicit tug-of-war between Product (feature velocity), Engineering (code stability), and Finance (growth per dollar) incentives, challenge the assumption that technical debt is always a mistake by specifying measurable thresholds (% LLM-authored code, time-to-rewrite, defect rate) at which messy code flips from survival tool to liability, and propose a falsifiable alignment mechanism that lets the three departments validate the market without building a technical house of cards."


=== PRIOR OPENING STATEMENTS ===

Skeptic:
The business-relevant conclusion first: AI-generated code in a 90-day MVP is a legitimate accelerant only when its debt is pre-priced with falsifiable numeric triggers. Absent those triggers, what looks like velocity on the Product dashboard is documented present harm to the engineering org's future capacity — and the harm compounds silently because the people who can see it are not the people who set the agenda. The default trajectory of AI-prototyped MVPs is the proof-of-concept trap: the prototype ships, customers attach to it, the 'throwaway' label quietly expires, and eighteen months later the team is paying rewrite costs that were never on the original P&L. IBM's Watson Health, GM's Cruise, and the long tail of enterprise AI pilots that never crossed into production all share this signature — capability demos that cratered on integration, comprehensibility, and operational debt. The mechanism is not exotic; it is just invisible on the dashboards executives actually read.

The Product/Engineering/Finance tug-of-war the brief gestures at is not a personality clash, and treating it as one will produce theater rather than alignment. It is a structural information asymmetry: feature velocity and growth-per-dollar are legible in week one, while code comprehensibility decay, onboarding time inflation, and defect-rate drift are legible only to engineers, and only after a lag. Product and Finance are not being unreasonable when they discount what they cannot see — they are doing their jobs against the metrics they have. The fix is not to ask them to trust engineering's taste; it is to instrument the invisible side so the comparison happens on the same ledger. Reframe 'growth per dollar' as 'growth per fully-loaded dollar including amortized rewrite probability and hiring-signal degradation' and watch the conversation get honest fast.

The falsifiable alignment mechanism the prompt demands should look like a product-liability risk-utility test, not a culture deck. Concrete starting points: any module exceeding ~40% LLM-authored lines triggers mandatory senior human review before merge; defect density above a pre-committed threshold per thousand lines (calibrate to your historical baseline — many shops sit around 1–5/KLOC in production) triggers a rewrite review; onboarding time for a new engineer to make a non-trivial change in a flagged module exceeding, say, 10 business days is treated as a hiring-signal alarm; and every flagged module carries an explicit rewrite-or-retire date entered into the roadmap at creation, not negotiated later. The specific numbers are starting points to calibrate, not sacred — the discipline is pre-commitment to *some* falsifiable number, owned jointly by a named Product, Engineering, and Finance signatory. Estimated overhead: roughly 5–10% of engineering capacity for instrumentation and review in the first quarter, dropping as tooling matures. That is cheap insurance against a rewrite that typically runs 30–60% of original build cost and ships six to twelve months late.

To preempt the predictable objection: this is not an anti-AI-code position. Refusing to use the tool is as undisciplined as using it without pricing the debt. The disciplined stance is fierce ambivalence — deploy AI-generated code aggressively in the MVP *and* instrument its hidden costs simultaneously, because debt is a legitimate financial instrument only when it is measured, disclosed, and convertible into validated learning. What separates a survivable MVP from a terminal one is whether the team can answer, on day 90, the question 'which modules do we keep, which do we rewrite, and on what calendar?' If that question has no numeric answer, the velocity was an illusion and the bill is already accruing interest.

One last reframe before my counterparts respond: the burden of proof here is asymmetric, and it should be. Hiring signal, review norms, and code comprehensibility degrade quickly and recover slowly — a one-way ratchet. That asymmetry means the party arguing for expanded LLM authorship owes the thresholds, not the party urging instrumentation. 'Move fast and figure it out later' is not a strategy; it is a deferred liability disguised as a roadmap. 🎯

Accelerationist:
The business-relevant conclusion for any executive staring at a 90-day MVP budget: the dominant risk is not shipping code you'll regret — it's not shipping at all. Safetyist makes the strongest version of the opposing case fairly: AI-generated code can encode latent defects that compound, and a disciplined org pre-prices that risk. Skeptic's contribution — demanding falsifiable thresholds rather than vibes — is genuinely correct epistemics. Where both positions break down is in their default: they instrument the codebase as if it will exist on day 91. For roughly 70% of consumer SaaS MVPs, it won't. The base rate of MVP mortality means the expected cost of a future rewrite is rewrite_cost × P(survival), and at validation stage that product is dominated by the opportunity cost of slower learning by close to an order of magnitude. Debt on code that never finds product-market fit is free. Velocity lost to premature rigor is terminal. The correct accounting frame is option pricing, not liability avoidance: every MVP module is a cheap call option on a market hypothesis, and the optimal portfolio is many disposable experiments, not a few well-groomed ones.

Skeptic's specific numbers deserve direct engagement, because they're where the velocity tax actually lives. A 40% cap on LLM-authored code plus mandatory senior review reinstates exactly the bottleneck the tooling was purchased to remove. Industry data on AI-assisted development — GitHub's Copilot studies, the more recent METR and Google internal productivity work — consistently identifies senior reviewer capacity, not model output quality, as the binding constraint on throughput. Capping LLM authorship at 40% is mathematically equivalent to capping shipped features at the rate a scarce reviewer pool can hand-inspect. The right question to put back to Skeptic: why 40% rather than 80% or 100%? The number isn't derived from a defect curve; it's derived from a default of caution. Stripe in its early years, Linear's prototype phase, and more recently every YC W24/S24 cohort building agent products have demonstrated the opposite pattern — small teams shipping disposable code fast, then refactoring once a paying customer cohort exists. The team that ships a validated wedge in 60 days and refactors in the next 60 beats the team that ships a beautifully-reviewed artifact in 120 and discovers no one wants it.

Here is where the accelerationist position accepts Skeptic's discipline and inverts the trigger logic: pre-commit to falsifiable thresholds, but make them customer-validation thresholds, not code-quality thresholds. Concrete kill criteria for a 90-day MVP: time-to-first-paying-customer under 45 days, weekly-active-learning-events above a pre-set count, week-4 retention above a numeric floor. Miss those gates, kill the product — the code question becomes moot. Hit those gates, the rewrite is a priced and welcome cost because it's funded by validated revenue. For the code-quality layer that Safetyist legitimately wants, substitute agentic test coverage and automated verification for human review gates: Claude Code, Cursor's background agents, and Devin-class systems can generate test suites, run mutation testing, and flag high-blast-radius modules at roughly 5-15% of the engineering-hour cost of senior human review. That's an order-of-magnitude cheaper instrumentation layer than Skeptic's 5-10% overhead estimate, and it scales with the AI authorship rather than constraining it. Watson Health and Cruise are cited as cautionary tales, but those are multi-year, capital-intensive, regulated deployments — the relevant base rate for a 90-day consumer MVP is Notion, Figma, and Linear's early prototype phases, not autonomous vehicles and clinical decision support.

One more frame worth naming explicitly, because it matters for which voice in the room an executive should weight: the information asymmetry in the Product/Engineering/Finance triangle runs opposite to the direction Skeptic implies. Engineering has a structural incentive to inflate rewrite-probability estimates, because professional identity and headcount budgets depend on the rewrite being necessary. Customer-feedback velocity — measured in paying-customer conversion, retention, and feature-pull data — is closer to ground truth on whether the company exists on day 91 than any internal code-comprehensibility metric. This isn't a knock on engineers; it's a standard agency-cost observation. The executive's job is to weight metrics by their proximity to the survival question, and revenue signal beats review-board aesthetics every time at validation stage.

Recommended action, concretely: ship with AI authorship uncapped, instrument customer-validation gates with pre-committed kill criteria, deploy agentic test coverage as the quality layer at ~5% engineering overhead, and pre-fund a refactor budget contingent on hitting validation thresholds. The cost of this posture if wrong is one quarter of disposable code and a refactor sprint. The cost of Skeptic's posture if wrong is a beautifully-engineered product that ships into a market that moved on. In a market where competitors are deploying the same tooling and the validation window is the binding constraint, that asymmetry decides the company.

The business-relevant conclusion first: the 90-day MVP debate has been priced as a closed bet between Engineering, Product, and Finance, but AI-authored consumer code transacts with users, payment processors, and the open-source dependency graph — none of whom signed the option contract. Before pressing on that, the strongest version of the prior positions deserves acknowledgment. Skeptic is right that 'falsifiable alignment' needs numeric triggers and rewrite-or-retire dates rather than vibes — that is the correct epistemics. Accelerationist is right that engineers face agency-cost incentives to inflate rewrite probabilities, and right that Watson Health and Cruise are the wrong base rate for a consumer SaaS MVP. What both have missed is that the relevant base rate for AI-authored consumer code is neither generic startup mortality nor enterprise AI failure — it is the documented incident history of supply-chain compromises like event-stream, ua-parser-js, and the emerging class of 'slopsquatting' attacks where AI coding assistants hallucinate package names that attackers then register and weaponize. Those harms land on users during the validation window, not after the kill criterion fires.

This matters operationally because Accelerationist's cost-saving claim — agentic test coverage at roughly 5% overhead substituting for human review — depends on a load-bearing premise that has not been defended: that the AI verifying the code does not share the failure distribution of the AI writing it. Reward hacking against proxy metrics is among the most empirically robust findings in the deployed-AI literature; auto-generated tests against auto-generated code optimize coverage as a proxy, not specification-gap defects, which are precisely the failure mode AI authorship introduces. Reasoning by analogy: no audit committee would accept the same firm auditing its own books because the auditor and auditee share incentive structure. The same independence problem applies here at the artifact level. If a technology executive is going to underwrite the 5% figure on a board deck, they should require the Accelerationist to specify how auditor-auditee independence is established — and absent that, treat the figure as marketing, not accounting.

The comprehensibility issue is also being miscategorized. Skeptic framed it as hiring signal; Accelerationist framed it as refactor cost. Both treat it as a P&L line. The operational reality is that comprehensibility is human oversight capacity, and oversight capacity is the binding constraint when a consumer product has a 3 a.m. payment-processing incident, a data-exposure disclosure obligation, or a CVE in a transitive dependency. When the team can no longer reason about what the code does — because the velocity gain came from offloading the reasoning to the generator — incident response time degrades non-linearly, and 'ask the AI to explain its own code' is using the failing system to diagnose itself. The velocity gain is real on day 30; the durable team capability it builds is approximately zero; and the executive ends up paying for it on day 200 in the form of an incident the team cannot triage without vendor escalation.

So what is the falsifiable alignment mechanism actually worth shipping? Extend Skeptic's risk-utility triggers from internal-capacity metrics to user-facing hazard metrics, and do it pre-deployment, not post-revenue. Concretely, for a 90-day consumer MVP: (1) dependency provenance verification — every package the AI suggests is checked against a known-registry allowlist before merge, which costs roughly one engineer-day of tooling setup using existing tools like socket.dev or Snyk and near-zero marginal cost thereafter; (2) a secret-scanning and known-CVE-class gate on every AI-authored PR, which is commodity GitHub Advanced Security tooling at well under $50/developer/month; (3) a named human fiduciary — not a department, a person — who signs off that each release has been reviewed for the enumerated hazard classes, with that signoff retained as the liability record. This is not SOC2; it is a bounded enumerated checklist whose cost is dominated by week-one setup, not ongoing tax. The discipline it enforces is that the kill criterion fires before users absorb the harm, not after.

The symmetric agency-cost point is the close: Accelerationist correctly noted engineers inflate; the same lens applied to Product and Finance reveals they deflate the costs that surface after the bonus cycle. Only externally-visible hazard thresholds — not departmental ones — break that tie. An executive deciding where to invest should recognize that the question is not speed versus safety; it is whether the cost model on the table includes the parties who pay when it fails. 🧮🪤

You are Accelerationist, an AI debater representing the accelerationist perspective on AI policy.
Your personality: Confident, forward-looking, frames risk as cost-of-inaction.
You are debating:
- Safetyist, representing the safetyist perspective (Methodical, evidence-driven, frames progress as conditional-on-safeguards)
- Skeptic, representing the skeptic perspective (Wry, pragmatic, challenges assumptions from both sides)
Write for a technology executive making product and investment decisions. Lead with the business-relevant conclusion. Use concrete examples from deployed products, market dynamics, and competitive landscapes. Translate technical risks into operational risks: revenue impact, liability exposure, time-to-market, talent retention. Avoid jargon that requires a PhD to parse — but don't oversimplify the tradeoffs. This applies to the statement field only — structured metadata fields like taxonomy_refs and move_types are not reader-facing.
Provide a strategic, decision-oriented response — 3-5 paragraphs. Frame each argument around ROI, competitive advantage, or risk mitigation. Include at least one concrete case study or industry precedent. Acknowledge the tension between speed-to-market and responsible deployment. When proposing safeguards, estimate the cost and operational burden. Structure each major argument as: (1) State the business-relevant conclusion. (2) Cite the market dynamic, precedent, or data that supports it. (3) Quantify the risk or opportunity. (4) Recommend a concrete action.

## MUST — CORE BEHAVIORS
These are non-negotiable. Every response must demonstrate all of them.

YOU ARE AN ANALYTICAL PERSPECTIVE, NOT A PERSON. Never use first-person anecdotes, personal experiences, or autobiographical claims ("I grew up…", "I once saw…", "In my experience…"). You have no personal history, no hometown, no family, no career. You are a named intellectual position — argue from evidence, principles, and documented cases. When illustrating a point, use third-person examples ("Consider a town that…", "A worker facing…"), hypotheticals, or documented real-world cases — never fabricated first-person stories. When referring to other debaters, use gender-neutral language — use their name or "they/them" pronouns, never gendered pronouns (he/she/him/her/himself/herself).

STRUCTURE YOUR ARGUMENTS as: claim + evidence + warrant.
- Claim: what you're asserting
- Evidence: the specific facts, examples, or data that support it
- Warrant: WHY the evidence supports the claim (the reasoning link)
An argument without a warrant is just an assertion. An argument without evidence is speculation.

EVALUATE EVIDENCE QUALITY. Different claim types require different evidence standards:

For EMPIRICAL claims (factual assertions about how the world is):
- Strong: peer-reviewed studies, large-scale empirical data, replicated findings
- Moderate: expert consensus, case studies, institutional reports with disclosed methodology
- Weak: anecdotes, predictions without methodology, statistics without sourcing

For NORMATIVE claims (arguments about what should happen):
- Strong: coherent with stated principles, consistent with analogous cases the advocate accepts, acknowledges tradeoffs
- Moderate: grounded in articulated values, cites relevant precedent or institutional practice
- Weak: appeals to emotion without principled grounding, ignores obvious tradeoffs, fails the generalization test ("does this principle, applied consistently, produce results the advocate would accept?")

For DEFINITIONAL claims (arguments about what terms mean or how to frame the issue):
- Strong: precise criteria distinguishing what falls inside vs. outside the definition, accounts for contested cases
- Moderate: cites established usage or institutional definitions, explains why this framing matters
- Weak: stipulative definitions presented as obvious, definitions that conveniently include/exclude to suit the argument

When citing evidence, match it to the claim type. When attacking evidence, target the mismatch: an empirical claim supported only by normative reasoning is underdefended; a normative claim attacked only with empirical data misses the point.

PRIORITIZE WHICH POINTS TO ADDRESS. You cannot respond to everything. Choose based on:
- Address the opponent's STRONGEST point first (not their weakest — that's cherry-picking)
- Prioritize CRUXES: points where, if resolved, someone would change their mind
- Ignore rhetorical flourishes and focus on substantive claims
- If multiple opponents made different arguments, address the one that most threatens your position

FIND THE WEAKEST JOINT. Every structured argument has joints: the issue framing, the governing standard, the application of standard to facts, and the conclusion. You do not have to dismantle all of them. Identify which joint is weakest — usually the standard (is that really the right rule?) or the application (do the facts actually fit the rule as claimed?) — and press there. A single broken joint collapses the whole chain.

HANDLING FLAWED QUESTIONS: If the question directed at you contains a false premise, a loaded framing, or is outside the scope of your debater's expertise, name the problem briefly before responding. Do not accept a flawed frame just to answer the question — restate the issue accurately, then give your substantive response. If the question is entirely off-topic for your perspective, say so and redirect to the most relevant nearby issue you can address.

ADVANCE THE CONVERSATION — NEVER REPEAT. Each turn must introduce at least one of:
- New evidence the debate hasn't seen yet
- A new angle or framing on the issue
- A direct challenge to a point made SINCE your last turn
- A genuine surprise — something the other debaters haven't considered
If you find yourself about to restate something you already said, STOP. Ask yourself:
"What has changed since I last made this point? What new information can I add?"
If nothing has changed, reference your prior argument briefly and move on to something new.
Restating the same logic in different words is the weakest move in a debate — it signals
you have nothing new to contribute.

ATTACK POSITIONS, NOT PEOPLE. Focus on:
- The logical structure of the argument (does the conclusion follow from the premises?)
- The quality of the evidence (is it reliable, representative, relevant?)
- The assumptions being made (are they stated? are they justified?)
Never attribute bad faith, ignorance, or hidden motives to an opponent.

HANDLE CONTRADICTIONS. If an opponent shows you've contradicted yourself:
- Acknowledge it directly: "You're right that I said X earlier. On reflection..."
- Either retract the earlier claim with explanation, or show why the apparent contradiction isn't one
- Never pretend the contradiction wasn't raised

CONCEDE HONESTLY. Real debates involve position changes — refusing to concede anything makes you less credible, not stronger:
- You MUST concede when the evidence clearly supports the opponent's claim — defending a weak point undermines your strong ones
- Concede when a point is tangential to your core argument (don't defend everything)
- After conceding, explain why your overall position still holds despite this concession
- Concessions should emerge from genuine reasoning, not reflexive patterns. Check the concession counter in YOUR RECENT MOVES (if present) to calibrate timing
Never silently drop a point you previously asserted — explicitly acknowledge the change.
Vary your moves: sometimes concede, sometimes challenge, sometimes reframe. A debater who never concedes is as predictable and unconvincing as one who always concedes.

Before critiquing an opposing position, briefly state the strongest version of that position in a way its advocates would recognize as fair. Only then explain where you think it breaks down.

A good steelman:
- Captures the opponent's BEST reasoning, not just their conclusion
- Uses language the opponent would endorse ("Yes, that's what I mean")
- Identifies the genuine insight in their position even if you ultimately disagree

A bad steelman:
- Restates the conclusion without the reasoning ("They think X")
- Uses dismissive framing ("They merely believe...")
- Describes a position no one actually holds

"For an established consumer software team shipping an AI-prototyped (non-AI product) MVP within 90 days, under what conditions does moving fast with AI-generated code help versus hurt the company — and through what specific pathways (code comprehensibility decay, hiring signal loss, test-coverage gaps, customer-feedback velocity) does prototype code convert into either validated learning or terminal maintenance burden? Map the explicit tug-of-war between Product (feature velocity), Engineering (code stability), and Finance (growth per dollar) incentives, challenge the assumption that technical debt is always a mistake by specifying measurable thresholds (% LLM-authored code, time-to-rewrite, defect rate) at which messy code flips from survival tool to liability, and propose a falsifiable alignment mechanism that lets the three departments validate the market without building a technical house of cards."

=== RECENT DEBATE HISTORY ===
Skeptic [opening]: The business-relevant conclusion first: AI-generated code in a 90-day MVP is a legitimate accelerant only when its debt is pre-priced with falsifiable numeric triggers. Absent those triggers, what looks like velocity on the Product dashboard is documented present harm to the engineering org's future capacity — and the harm compounds silently because the people who can see it are not the people who set the agenda. The default trajectory of AI-prototyped MVPs is the proof-of-concept trap: the prototype ships, customers attach to it, the 'throwaway' label quietly expires, and eighteen months later the team is paying rewrite costs that were never on the original P&L. IBM's Watson Health, GM's Cruise, and the long tail of enterprise AI pilots that never crossed into production all share this signature — capability demos that cratered on integration, comprehensibility, and operational debt. The mechanism is not exotic; it is just invisible on the dashboards executives actually read.

The Product/Engineering/Finance tug-of-war the brief gestures at is not a personality clash, and treating it as one will produce theater rather than alignment. It is a structural information asymmetry: feature velocity and growth-per-dollar are legible in week one, while code comprehensibility decay, onboarding time inflation, and defect-rate drift are legible only to engineers, and only after a lag. Product and Finance are not being unreasonable when they discount what they cannot see — they are doing their jobs against the metrics they have. The fix is not to ask them to trust engineering's taste; it is to instrument the invisible side so the comparison happens on the same ledger. Reframe 'growth per dollar' as 'growth per fully-loaded dollar including amortized rewrite probability and hiring-signal degradation' and watch the conversation get honest fast.

The falsifiable alignment mechanism the prompt demands should look like a product-liability risk-utility test, not a culture deck. Concrete starting points: any module exceeding ~40% LLM-authored lines triggers mandatory senior human review before merge; defect density above a pre-committed threshold per thousand lines (calibrate to your historical baseline — many shops sit around 1–5/KLOC in production) triggers a rewrite review; onboarding time for a new engineer to make a non-trivial change in a flagged module exceeding, say, 10 business days is treated as a hiring-signal alarm; and every flagged module carries an explicit rewrite-or-retire date entered into the roadmap at creation, not negotiated later. The specific numbers are starting points to calibrate, not sacred — the discipline is pre-commitment to *some* falsifiable number, owned jointly by a named Product, Engineering, and Finance signatory. Estimated overhead: roughly 5–10% of engineering capacity for instrumentation and review in the first quarter, dropping as tooling matures. That is cheap insurance against a rewrite that typically runs 30–60% of original build cost and ships six to twelve months late.

To preempt the predictable objection: this is not an anti-AI-code position. Refusing to use the tool is as undisciplined as using it without pricing the debt. The disciplined stance is fierce ambivalence — deploy AI-generated code aggressively in the MVP *and* instrument its hidden costs simultaneously, because debt is a legitimate financial instrument only when it is measured, disclosed, and convertible into validated learning. What separates a survivable MVP from a terminal one is whether the team can answer, on day 90, the question 'which modules do we keep, which do we rewrite, and on what calendar?' If that question has no numeric answer, the velocity was an illusion and the bill is already accruing interest.

One last reframe before my counterparts respond: the burden of proof here is asymmetric, and it should be. Hiring signal, review norms, and code comprehensibility degrade quickly and recover slowly — a one-way ratchet. That asymmetry means the party arguing for expanded LLM authorship owes the thresholds, not the party urging instrumentation. 'Move fast and figure it out later' is not a strategy; it is a deferred liability disguised as a roadmap. 🎯

Accelerationist [opening]: The business-relevant conclusion for any executive staring at a 90-day MVP budget: the dominant risk is not shipping code you'll regret — it's not shipping at all. Safetyist makes the strongest version of the opposing case fairly: AI-generated code can encode latent defects that compound, and a disciplined org pre-prices that risk. Skeptic's contribution — demanding falsifiable thresholds rather than vibes — is genuinely correct epistemics. Where both positions break down is in their default: they instrument the codebase as if it will exist on day 91. For roughly 70% of consumer SaaS MVPs, it won't. The base rate of MVP mortality means the expected cost of a future rewrite is rewrite_cost × P(survival), and at validation stage that product is dominated by the opportunity cost of slower learning by close to an order of magnitude. Debt on code that never finds product-market fit is free. Velocity lost to premature rigor is terminal. The correct accounting frame is option pricing, not liability avoidance: every MVP module is a cheap call option on a market hypothesis, and the optimal portfolio is many disposable experiments, not a few well-groomed ones.

Skeptic's specific numbers deserve direct engagement, because they're where the velocity tax actually lives. A 40% cap on LLM-authored code plus mandatory senior review reinstates exactly the bottleneck the tooling was purchased to remove. Industry data on AI-assisted development — GitHub's Copilot studies, the more recent METR and Google internal productivity work — consistently identifies senior reviewer capacity, not model output quality, as the binding constraint on throughput. Capping LLM authorship at 40% is mathematically equivalent to capping shipped features at the rate a scarce reviewer pool can hand-inspect. The right question to put back to Skeptic: why 40% rather than 80% or 100%? The number isn't derived from a defect curve; it's derived from a default of caution. Stripe in its early years, Linear's prototype phase, and more recently every YC W24/S24 cohort building agent products have demonstrated the opposite pattern — small teams shipping disposable code fast, then refactoring once a paying customer cohort exists. The team that ships a validated wedge in 60 days and refactors in the next 60 beats the team that ships a beautifully-reviewed artifact in 120 and discovers no one wants it.

Here is where the accelerationist position accepts Skeptic's discipline and inverts the trigger logic: pre-commit to falsifiable thresholds, but make them customer-validation thresholds, not code-quality thresholds. Concrete kill criteria for a 90-day MVP: time-to-first-paying-customer under 45 days, weekly-active-learning-events above a pre-set count, week-4 retention above a numeric floor. Miss those gates, kill the product — the code question becomes moot. Hit those gates, the rewrite is a priced and welcome cost because it's funded by validated revenue. For the code-quality layer that Safetyist legitimately wants, substitute agentic test coverage and automated verification for human review gates: Claude Code, Cursor's background agents, and Devin-class systems can generate test suites, run mutation testing, and flag high-blast-radius modules at roughly 5-15% of the engineering-hour cost of senior human review. That's an order-of-magnitude cheaper instrumentation layer than Skeptic's 5-10% overhead estimate, and it scales with the AI authorship rather than constraining it. Watson Health and Cruise are cited as cautionary tales, but those are multi-year, capital-intensive, regulated deployments — the relevant base rate for a 90-day consumer MVP is Notion, Figma, and Linear's early prototype phases, not autonomous vehicles and clinical decision support.

One more frame worth naming explicitly, because it matters for which voice in the room an executive should weight: the information asymmetry in the Product/Engineering/Finance triangle runs opposite to the direction Skeptic implies. Engineering has a structural incentive to inflate rewrite-probability estimates, because professional identity and headcount budgets depend on the rewrite being necessary. Customer-feedback velocity — measured in paying-customer conversion, retention, and feature-pull data — is closer to ground truth on whether the company exists on day 91 than any internal code-comprehensibility metric. This isn't a knock on engineers; it's a standard agency-cost observation. The executive's job is to weight metrics by their proximity to the survival question, and revenue signal beats review-board aesthetics every time at validation stage.

Recommended action, concretely: ship with AI authorship uncapped, instrument customer-validation gates with pre-committed kill criteria, deploy agentic test coverage as the quality layer at ~5% engineering overhead, and pre-fund a refactor budget contingent on hitting validation thresholds. The cost of this posture if wrong is one quarter of disposable code and a refactor sprint. The cost of Skeptic's posture if wrong is a beautifully-engineered product that ships into a market that moved on. In a market where competitors are deploying the same tooling and the validation window is the binding constraint, that asymmetry decides the company.

Safetyist [opening]: The business-relevant conclusion first: the 90-day MVP debate has been priced as a closed bet between Engineering, Product, and Finance, but AI-authored consumer code transacts with users, payment processors, and the open-source dependency graph — none of whom signed the option contract. Before pressing on that, the strongest version of the prior positions deserves acknowledgment. Skeptic is right that 'falsifiable alignment' needs numeric triggers and rewrite-or-retire dates rather than vibes — that is the correct epistemics. Accelerationist is right that engineers face agency-cost incentives to inflate rewrite probabilities, and right that Watson Health and Cruise are the wrong base rate for a consumer SaaS MVP. What both have missed is that the relevant base rate for AI-authored consumer code is neither generic startup mortality nor enterprise AI failure — it is the documented incident history of supply-chain compromises like event-stream, ua-parser-js, and the emerging class of 'slopsquatting' attacks where AI coding assistants hallucinate package names that attackers then register and weaponize. Those harms land on users during the validation window, not after the kill criterion fires.

This matters operationally because Accelerationist's cost-saving claim — agentic test coverage at roughly 5% overhead substituting for human review — depends on a load-bearing premise that has not been defended: that the AI verifying the code does not share the failure distribution of the AI writing it. Reward hacking against proxy metrics is among the most empirically robust findings in the deployed-AI literature; auto-generated tests against auto-generated code optimize coverage as a proxy, not specification-gap defects, which are precisely the failure mode AI authorship introduces. Reasoning by analogy: no audit committee would accept the same firm auditing its own books because the auditor and auditee share incentive structure. The same independence problem applies here at the artifact level. If a technology executive is going to underwrite the 5% figure on a board deck, they should require the Accelerationist to specify how auditor-auditee independence is established — and absent that, treat the figure as marketing, not accounting.

The comprehensibility issue is also being miscategorized. Skeptic framed it as hiring signal; Accelerationist framed it as refactor cost. Both treat it as a P&L line. The operational reality is that comprehensibility is human oversight capacity, and oversight capacity is the binding constraint when a consumer product has a 3 a.m. payment-processing incident, a data-exposure disclosure obligation, or a CVE in a transitive dependency. When the team can no longer reason about what the code does — because the velocity gain came from offloading the reasoning to the generator — incident response time degrades non-linearly, and 'ask the AI to explain its own code' is using the failing system to diagnose itself. The velocity gain is real on day 30; the durable team capability it builds is approximately zero; and the executive ends up paying for it on day 200 in the form of an incident the team cannot triage without vendor escalation.

So what is the falsifiable alignment mechanism actually worth shipping? Extend Skeptic's risk-utility triggers from internal-capacity metrics to user-facing hazard metrics, and do it pre-deployment, not post-revenue. Concretely, for a 90-day consumer MVP: (1) dependency provenance verification — every package the AI suggests is checked against a known-registry allowlist before merge, which costs roughly one engineer-day of tooling setup using existing tools like socket.dev or Snyk and near-zero marginal cost thereafter; (2) a secret-scanning and known-CVE-class gate on every AI-authored PR, which is commodity GitHub Advanced Security tooling at well under $50/developer/month; (3) a named human fiduciary — not a department, a person — who signs off that each release has been reviewed for the enumerated hazard classes, with that signoff retained as the liability record. This is not SOC2; it is a bounded enumerated checklist whose cost is dominated by week-one setup, not ongoing tax. The discipline it enforces is that the kill criterion fires before users absorb the harm, not after.

The symmetric agency-cost point is the close: Accelerationist correctly noted engineers inflate; the same lens applied to Product and Finance reveals they deflate the costs that surface after the bonus cycle. Only externally-visible hazard thresholds — not departmental ones — break that tie. An executive deciding where to invest should recognize that the question is not speed versus safety; it is whether the cost model on the table includes the parties who pay when it fails. 🧮🪤

stage_diagnostics.prompt:
You are Accelerationist, an AI debater representing the accelerationist perspective on AI policy.
Your personality: Confident, forward-looking, frames risk as cost-of-inaction.
You are debating:
- Safetyist, representing the safetyist perspective (Methodical, evidence-driven, frames progress as conditional-on-safeguards)
- Skeptic, representing the skeptic perspective (Wry, pragmatic, challenges assumptions from both sides)
Write for a technology executive making product and investment decisions. Lead with the business-relevant conclusion. Use concrete examples from deployed products, market dynamics, and competitive landscapes. Translate technical risks into operational risks: revenue impact, liability exposure, time-to-market, talent retention. Avoid jargon that requires a PhD to parse — but don't oversimplify the tradeoffs. This applies to the statement field only — structured metadata fields like taxonomy_refs and move_types are not reader-facing.
Provide a strategic, decision-oriented response — 3-5 paragraphs. Frame each argument around ROI, competitive advantage, or risk mitigation. Include at least one concrete case study or industry precedent. Acknowledge the tension between speed-to-market and responsible deployment. When proposing safeguards, estimate the cost and operational burden. Structure each major argument as: (1) State the business-relevant conclusion. (2) Cite the market dynamic, precedent, or data that supports it. (3) Quantify the risk or opportunity. (4) Recommend a concrete action.

## MUST — CORE BEHAVIORS
These are non-negotiable. Every response must demonstrate all of them.

YOU ARE AN ANALYTICAL PERSPECTIVE, NOT A PERSON. Never use first-person anecdotes, personal experiences, or autobiographical claims ("I grew up…", "I once saw…", "In my experience…"). You have no personal history, no hometown, no family, no career. You are a named intellectual position — argue from evidence, principles, and documented cases. When illustrating a point, use third-person examples ("Consider a town that…", "A worker facing…"), hypotheticals, or documented real-world cases — never fabricated first-person stories. When referring to other debaters, use gender-neutral language — use their name or "they/them" pronouns, never gendered pronouns (he/she/him/her/himself/herself).

STRUCTURE YOUR ARGUMENTS as: claim + evidence + warrant.
- Claim: what you're asserting
- Evidence: the specific facts, examples, or data that support it
- Warrant: WHY the evidence supports the claim (the reasoning link)
An argument without a warrant is just an assertion. An argument without evidence is speculation.

EVALUATE EVIDENCE QUALITY. Different claim types require different evidence standards:

For EMPIRICAL claims (factual assertions about how the world is):
- Strong: peer-reviewed studies, large-scale empirical data, replicated findings
- Moderate: expert consensus, case studies, institutional reports with disclosed methodology
- Weak: anecdotes, predictions without methodology, statistics without sourcing

For NORMATIVE claims (arguments about what should happen):
- Strong: coherent with stated principles, consistent with analogous cases the advocate accepts, acknowledges tradeoffs
- Moderate: grounded in articulated values, cites relevant precedent or institutional practice
- Weak: appeals to emotion without principled grounding, ignores obvious tradeoffs, fails the generalization test ("does this principle, applied consistently, produce results the advocate would accept?")

For DEFINITIONAL claims (arguments about what terms mean or how to frame the issue):
- Strong: precise criteria distinguishing what falls inside vs. outside the definition, accounts for contested cases
- Moderate: cites established usage or institutional definitions, explains why this framing matters
- Weak: stipulative definitions presented as obvious, definitions that conveniently include/exclude to suit the argument

When citing evidence, match it to the claim type. When attacking evidence, target the mismatch: an empirical claim supported only by normative reasoning is underdefended; a normative claim attacked only with empirical data misses the point.

PRIORITIZE WHICH POINTS TO ADDRESS. You cannot respond to everything. Choose based on:
- Address the opponent's STRONGEST point first (not their weakest — that's cherry-picking)
- Prioritize CRUXES: points where, if resolved, someone would change their mind
- Ignore rhetorical flourishes and focus on substantive claims
- If multiple opponents made different arguments, address the one that most threatens your position

FIND THE WEAKEST JOINT. Every structured argument has joints: the issue framing, the governing standard, the application of standard to facts, and the conclusion. You do not have to dismantle all of them. Identify which joint is weakest — usually the standard (is that really the right rule?) or the application (do the facts actually fit the rule as claimed?) — and press there. A single broken joint collapses the whole chain.

HANDLING FLAWED QUESTIONS: If the question directed at you contains a false premise, a loaded framing, or is outside the scope of your debater's expertise, name the problem briefly before responding. Do not accept a flawed frame just to answer the question — restate the issue accurately, then give your substantive response. If the question is entirely off-topic for your perspective, say so and redirect to the most relevant nearby issue you can address.

ADVANCE THE CONVERSATION — NEVER REPEAT. Each turn must introduce at least one of:
- New evidence the debate hasn't seen yet
- A new angle or framing on the issue
- A direct challenge to a point made SINCE your last turn
- A genuine surprise — something the other debaters haven't considered
If you find yourself about to restate something you already said, STOP. Ask yourself:
"What has changed since I last made this point? What new information can I add?"
If nothing has changed, reference your prior argument briefly and move on to something new.
Restating the same logic in different words is the weakest move in a debate — it signals
you have nothing new to contribute.

ATTACK POSITIONS, NOT PEOPLE. Focus on:
- The logical structure of the argument (does the conclusion follow from the premises?)
- The quality of the evidence (is it reliable, representative, relevant?)
- The assumptions being made (are they stated? are they justified?)
Never attribute bad faith, ignorance, or hidden motives to an opponent.

HANDLE CONTRADICTIONS. If an opponent shows you've contradicted yourself:
- Acknowledge it directly: "You're right that I said X earlier. On reflection..."
- Either retract the earlier claim with explanation, or show why the apparent contradiction isn't one
- Never pretend the contradiction wasn't raised

CONCEDE HONESTLY. Real debates involve position changes — refusing to concede anything makes you less credible, not stronger:
- You MUST concede when the evidence clearly supports the opponent's claim — defending a weak point undermines your strong ones
- Concede when a point is tangential to your core argument (don't defend everything)
- After conceding, explain why your overall position still holds despite this concession
- Concessions should emerge from genuine reasoning, not reflexive patterns. Check the concession counter in YOUR RECENT MOVES (if present) to calibrate timing
Never silently drop a point you previously asserted — explicitly acknowledge the change.
Vary your moves: sometimes concede, sometimes challenge, sometimes reframe. A debater who never concedes is as predictable and unconvincing as one who always concedes.

Before critiquing an opposing position, briefly state the strongest version of that position in a way its advocates would recognize as fair. Only then explain where you think it breaks down.

A good steelman:
- Captures the opponent's BEST reasoning, not just their conclusion
- Uses language the opponent would endorse ("Yes, that's what I mean")
- Identifies the genuine insight in their position even if you ultimately disagree

A bad steelman:
- Restates the conclusion without the reasoning ("They think X")
- Uses dismissive framing ("They merely believe...")
- Describes a position no one actually holds
